title: Pre-Analysis — Backplane Standard Against the Partition Memory Request
abstract: Closed work order testing whether the backplane standard could absorb a partition memory increase without a further module change, closed with the answer that it could not.

sections.objective: Establish whether the backplane and cooling standard could absorb an increase in module partition memory by a data change alone, as an operator had asked, or whether a further module change would be required. The commercial attraction of a data-only answer was obvious and the work order existed to test it rather than to assume it.
sections.findings_summary: It cannot. Partition memory is a property of the module, not of the backplane or of the configuration table, and the current module family has no headroom at two of the six slots. A data change can move an allocation between partitions but cannot create memory that is not there, and the two slots at ninety-four per cent are exactly the ones the next tranche of functions would land in. The backplane standard does help in one respect that had not been recognised: the cooling ducting it introduced creates enough thermal margin at those two slots to accept a higher-dissipation module later, which a delivered-backplane rack would not. That makes this standard a prerequisite for whatever comes next rather than a dead end. The installation task already reads the configuration from the terminal and would need to read a loadable table as well.
sections.next_steps: Answer the operator that a data-only route does not exist. Record the cooling margin as the reason this standard is a prerequisite for any successor. Hand the loadable table question to the successor definition.
